product.title: Taiwanese Mandarin 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero in Taiwanese Mandarin (國語): pīnyīn printed right above traditional characters 繁體字, short natural dialogues set in Taipei and Tainan, word-for-word translations that show how Mandarin builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary, exercises, and an answer key. Includes a pīnyīn chart, four-tone and tone-change practice, a table of 注音符號 (bopomofo) as used all over Taiwan, traditional vs. simplified characters, Taiwan vs. mainland vocabulary, an A1 grammar summary, and a glossary. Written for English speakers — each unit targets one common stumbling block, from measure words you can't skip to the 了 that isn't a past tense.

blocks.text: The language in this book is called **華語** (*Huáyǔ*) in Taiwan, **國語** (*Guóyǔ*) in schools and on the news, and **Mandarin** on your language certificate. All three are one language. Twenty-three million people speak it every day in Taiwan, and around one and a half billion people worldwide speak the same language with small differences — so every sentence you learn here is just as useful in Kuala Lumpur, Singapore, Beijing, or San Francisco's Chinatown.

So why a course just for Taiwan? Because of three things that make Taiwanese Mandarin feel different from day one, all of them in the things you use most: **the characters are traditional**, **the helper alphabet is not pīnyīn but 注音**, and **some everyday words are completely different** from those taught in books published in China. Someone who learned from a mainland textbook and lands at Taoyuan will understand almost everything — but will call a bicycle by a word that makes Taiwanese people smile, and won't be able to read a single shop sign.
Why Mandarin is kinder than you think
Mandarin's reputation as the world's hardest language is largely undeserved. Four things give English speakers a much shorter road than they expect.

items: **Verbs never change form.** No *eat/ate/eaten*, no *I eat / she eats*. *吃* is *吃* forever.
**No grammatical gender and no articles.** No *der/die/das*, no *a/the*. *書* can mean "book", "a book", or "the book" — context decides.
**Nouns don't change for plural.** *兩本書* = "two book", no "-s". The number says it all.
**The basic word order is the same: subject – verb – object.** *我喝茶* = "I drink tea". Word for word, the order is identical to English.

blocks.text: So where's the hard part?
In three places, all of them genuinely new to you. Better to know what they look like now so they don't catch you off guard.

items: **Tones.** The same syllable said with a different melody is a different word. *Mā* mother, *má* hemp, *mǎ* horse, *mà* scold. This isn't an accent or a speaking style — it's part of the word itself, as important as its letters. Two whole pages are waiting for you just ahead.

**Characters.** There are no letters. Every word is written with a symbol you have to recognize one by one. The good news: this book prints the pronunciation **right above** every character, so you never stumble, and the characters settle into your head through repetition, not forced memorization.

**Measure words.** English has "a cup of", "a piece of" — but lets you say "two books" with nothing in between. Mandarin gives you no such freedom. *兩本書*, not *兩書*. This is the number-one mistake for English speakers, and unit 5 tackles it head on.

blocks.text: What's special about Taiwan

This book writes everything in **traditional characters 繁體字**, as used in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau. They do have more strokes than the simplified characters used in mainland China, which sounds like a drawback — until you realize those extra strokes are what hold the clues to meaning and sound. *愛* (love) contains *心* (heart); its simplified form, *爱*, doesn't. Learners who start with traditional can read simplified in a few hours; the reverse isn't true.

The dialogues take place in real places: the Taipei 捷運, the 士林 night market, the tea shop across from campus, the train to 台南, a clinic with a 健保卡. There are two main characters: **Budi**, an exchange student from Indonesia, and **林小美 (Lín Xiǎoměi)**, his classmate from Taipei. You'll follow them through one semester.

blocks.title: What you can do after unit twenty
items: Read and pronounce pīnyīn correctly, including the four tones and the three tone-change rules.
Read the 注音 alphabet found in every Taiwanese dictionary and on every Taiwanese phone keyboard.
Recognize about 400 traditional characters and use about 600 words.
Order food and drinks with the sugar and ice you like, ride the 捷運 and the 高鐵, haggle at a night market, visit a clinic, and talk about your family for a full minute.

front.title: Contents
front.intro: Twenty units, each built to settle one point that most often trips up English speakers.

blocks.text: Each unit is designed for **one sitting of twenty to thirty minutes**. Don't do two units at once even if it feels easy — what drives your progress isn't how much you read today but how many days in a row you open this book.
Recommended order within a unit

items: **Read the dialogue once, look at the translation, close it.** Don't memorize anything.
**Read the dialogue again out loud**, this time following the pīnyīn above the characters. Exaggerate the tones — better to sound like you're singing than to sound flat.
**Read the notes and the grammar boxes.** That's where the unit's real content is; the dialogue is just the bait.
**Do the exercises without looking at the key.** The answers are at the end of the unit, and peeking early throws away all the benefit.
**Tomorrow, before starting a new unit, reread yesterday's dialogue once.** Thirty seconds, no more.

blocks.text: Reading a dialogue page

Every line of dialogue has three layers. **Above the characters** is the pīnyīn — how to say it. **Below the line** are two translations: the italic one with dashes is the **literal** translation, word for word, showing how Mandarin builds the sentence; the plain one is the **natural** English translation. The literal version often sounds odd, and that's the point — it's your real grammar teacher.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Three habits that decide whether you succeed
items: **Always say it out loud.** A tonal language can't be learned with your eyes. Your tongue has to learn it, not your eyes.
**Learn the tone with the word, from the very first word.** Learning *ma* first and adding the tone later is double work, and the second half never gets done. Learn *mā* as one complete sound.
**Don't jump to the characters.** Writing characters is fun and addictive, but at A1 what decides whether you can speak is tones and sentence patterns. The characters will come on their own.

blocks.text: The **⚠️** sign throughout the book marks the places where English speakers most often slip. Whenever you see it, pause for a moment — the next sentence usually saves you from a habit that's hard to undo once it has formed.

front.title: Pīnyīn: reading Mandarin in one sitting

blocks.text: **拼音** (*pīnyīn*) writes the sounds of Mandarin in Latin letters. It is not English spelling — it's a system of its own, and some letters sound very different from what you'd guess. Half an hour on this page will save you months of wrong pronunciation.

Every Mandarin syllable has three parts: an **initial** (consonant), a **final** (vowel and its tail), and a **tone**. There are 21 initials and 35 finals, and they combine into only about 400 syllables — a number you really can get through in one sitting.
The easy ones: close to English

blocks.text: ⚠️ **q, x, j are three siblings.** All three are said with **the tongue tip resting behind the lower teeth** and the middle of the tongue raised to the roof of the mouth. If your tongue tip goes up, you're saying *ch, sh, zh* — a different group altogether. Quickest way in: say "she" with a wide smile. That's *xi*. Add a stop in front: that's *ji*. Add a puff of air: that's *qi*.
Curled tongue: zh ch sh r
These four are said with **the tongue tip curled back** to touch the roof of the mouth. English has close cousins but none exactly the same, so all four need practice in front of a mirror.

blocks.title: Good news from Taiwan
items: **In Taiwan, the tongue curl is much lighter than in Beijing.** Many Taiwanese speakers say *zh, ch, sh* almost like *z, c, s*. *是* often sounds like *sù*, *知道* like *zīdào*.
That means your pronunciation doesn't have to match Beijing news anchors to sound natural in Taipei. Still **practice the curl** so you can hear it, but don't lose heart if it isn't perfect yet.

⚠️ One thing that really is different: **兒化 (érhuà)** — the Beijing habit of adding *-r* to the end of words (*哪儿 nǎr*) — **barely exists in Taiwan**. In Taiwan people say *哪裡 nǎlǐ*. Don't imitate it, or you'll sound like you're doing an impression of a mainland TV drama.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Watch the row **-i after z c s zh ch sh r**. This is the most stubborn trap: *四* (four) is not *see*, but an *s* held with a slight buzz. If you say it as *see*, Taiwanese people will hear *西* (west). Say *sì* and *xī* one after the other until you can hear the difference yourself.

front.title: Four tones, and three changes you must make

blocks.text: This is the part that's truly new to you, and the part that decides whether people in Taiwan understand you. Tones in Mandarin are **not intonation** — not the way you raise your voice at the end of a question. A tone is **part of the word**, just like its letters. Change the tone and you change the word.

head: Tone
Mark
Shape
Think of
Example
rows: the "aaah" at the doctor's when they check your throat
rises from the middle to the top
dips low, then rises a little
drops sharply from top to bottom
a last syllable tossed off in passing

blocks.text: The legendary sentence for practicing all five at once: **媽媽罵馬嗎？** *Māma mà mǎ ma?* — "Is Mom scolding the horse?" Say it ten times until it flows. Every *ma* in it is different.

blocks.title: ⚠️ The number-one mistake for English speakers
items: **Raising your voice at the end of a question.** In English, "You're eating?" is marked by a rising pitch. In Mandarin, a question is marked by the **word** 嗎 at the end — the pitch doesn't change at all. Raising the last syllable turns it into a different word.

**Saying a full third tone in the middle of a sentence.** The full third tone (down then up) only appears when the word stands alone or at the end of a sentence. In the middle, it just dips low and stays there.

**Using English word stress instead of tones.** English stresses one syllable and swallows the rest ("TEA-cher", "to-MOR-row"). Mandarin has no stress like that — each syllable has its own tone, and both count equally.

blocks.text: Change one: two third tones meet
When two third-tone syllables meet, **the first one changes to a second tone**. It's still written as a third tone; only the pronunciation changes.

This isn't a rule you need to memorize — it happens by itself as soon as you try to say two third tones quickly in a row. Try *nǐ hǎo* slowly, then faster and faster; your mouth will find it on its own.
Change two: 不 (bù)
**不** is normally fourth tone: *bù*. But when the next word is also fourth tone, it changes to second tone: *bú*.
Change three: 一 (yī)

head: Situation
Tone
Example
rows: On its own, counting, or at the end
*一杯 yì bēi* one cup, *一年 yì nián* one year
*一個 yí ge* one (of something), *一樣 yí yàng* the same

blocks.text: ⚠️ **This book writes 一 and 不 with the tone actually spoken**, not the dictionary tone. So you'll see *yí ge* and *bú shì* printed above the characters, and you just read what's there. Most Mandarin books print the dictionary tone and leave you to change it yourself — which is how beginners end up saying *yī ge* for years.

blocks.title: Five minutes of practice today
items: *mā – má – mǎ – mà* ten times, in order, out loud. Record yourself on your phone and listen back.
*yī – yí – yì*: *一 (yī), 一個 (yí ge), 一杯 (yì bēi)*.
*bù – bú*: *不好 (bù hǎo), 不是 (bú shì)*.
*nǐ hǎo* said fast ten times until the first syllable rises on its own.
⚠️ If one of them feels impossible today, leave it and come back tomorrow. Tones come through daily repetition, not one long session.

front.title: 注音符號: the alphabet all of Taiwan uses

blocks.text: Ask a Taiwanese child how to read a character and they won't write pīnyīn. They'll write **ㄅㄆㄇㄈ** — **注音符號** (*zhùyīn fúhào*), often shortened to **注音** or called **ㄅㄆㄇㄈ** (*bopomofo*) after its first four symbols, just as "alphabet" comes from alpha-beta.

This is no side issue. **Every primary school in Taiwan teaches 注音 before characters**, every Taiwanese dictionary uses it, every children's book prints it next to the characters, and **the phone keyboard most Taiwanese people use is a 注音 keyboard**. If you want to text a Taiwanese friend the way they do, you need to know it.

The good news: it's just **37 symbols**, one sound each, with no exceptions at all — far more honest than pīnyīn, which writes *ü* as *u* after j q x y and hides an *e* inside *ian* and *ui*. You can read it in an hour.
Initials: 21 symbols
Finals: 16 symbols

Tones are written as small marks alongside: first tone **no mark**, second tone **ˊ**, third tone **ˇ**, fourth tone **ˋ**, and the neutral tone **˙**, placed **in front**. ⚠️ Note that this is the reverse of pīnyīn: in pīnyīn, no mark means neutral tone; in 注音, no mark means first tone.

blocks.title: Do you need to learn it now?
items: **Not required for A1.** This book uses pīnyīn throughout so you can start reading and speaking right away.
**But highly recommended before you go to Taiwan.** Without 注音 you can't use a Taiwanese dictionary, can't read children's books, and can't type on the keyboard your friends use.
**The cheapest way:** add a 注音 keyboard to your phone today and just leave it there. Every time you type a word, you see the symbols. In two weeks they'll sink in without a single study session.
The full 注音 ↔ pīnyīn table is at the back of this book, ready to photograph and pin up.

front.title: 繁體字: traditional characters and how to tame them

blocks.text: Chinese characters aren't letters. They aren't pictures of things either — the idea that 山 is a "picture of a mountain" holds true only for the first few dozen characters. **About eighty-five percent of characters are built from two parts: one part hints at the meaning, the other at the sound.** Once you see that pattern, characters stop feeling like blind memorization.

Look at the last rows: **言 + 青 = 請** (to do with speech, sounding *qing*) and **氵 + 青 = 清** (to do with water, sounding *qing*). One shared sound part gives birth to a whole family of characters. That's how people recognize ten thousand characters without memorizing ten thousand times.

blocks.text: Traditional vs. simplified: what's the difference?

Mainland China simplified about two thousand characters in the 1950s; Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Macau did not follow. What did **not** change is the language — grammar, sounds, and most vocabulary are the same. Only the written form of some characters changed. And most characters are **exactly the same** in both systems: 我, 你, 是, 不, 在, 人, 大, 小, 天, 日, 月 were never simplified.

A longer list is at the back. ⚠️ The one thing you need to know now: **if you learn traditional first, reading simplified later takes just a few hours.** Simplified often merges several traditional characters into one form, so it's the other direction that causes trouble.

blocks.title: Stroke order: necessary or not?
items: **Yes, if you want to write by hand** — and handwriting is the most powerful way to remember characters.
There are only five core rules: **top before bottom**, **left before right**, **horizontal before downward**, **outside before inside**, **close the box last**.
⚠️ But at A1, **recognizing** characters is worth far more than **writing** them. If your time is limited, spend it on speaking.
If you do want to write: pick ten characters per unit and write each ten times while saying the sound out loud. Writing in silence only trains your hand.

blocks.text: English has borrowed a few dozen words from Chinese — most of them via **Hokkien** and **Cantonese**, the languages of the southern ports where Western traders first landed. Hokkien is also the mother tongue of most people in Taiwan. Because they came that way and not through Mandarin, the sounds are often far apart; but **the characters are exactly the same**, and seeing the link makes dozens of new words feel like old friends.

⚠️ Notice that the Mandarin sound is **not** the same as the English one. *Tea* comes from Hokkien *tê*, while Mandarin says *chá*. Don't say *dim sum* in Taipei and expect to be understood — say *diǎnxīn*. What's useful in this table isn't the sound but **the characters**: once you know 麵 means "noodles", you'll recognize it in 炒麵 (chow mein), 牛肉麵 (beef noodle soup), 泡麵 (instant noodles), and 麵包 (bread).

blocks.title: And words borrowed the other way
items: Mandarin also borrows from English, and the results are often funny but easy to guess: *咖啡 kāfēi* coffee, *巧克力 qiǎokèlì* chocolate, *沙發 shāfā* sofa, *披薩 pīsà* pizza.
*T恤 T-xù* T-shirt, *卡 kǎ* card, *吧 bā* bar, *的士 dìshì* taxi (⚠️ in Taiwan people say *計程車 jìchéngchē*).

⚠️ Some loanwords **differ between Taiwan and the mainland**: software is *軟體 ruǎntǐ* in Taiwan, *软件 ruǎnjiàn* on the mainland; network/internet is *網路 wǎnglù* in Taiwan, *网络 wǎngluò* on the mainland.
You'll meet words like these throughout the book; they're free gifts that speed up your vocabulary.

back.title: The measure words you must have

blocks.text: This is the wall that trips up English speakers most. The rule is one sentence: **between a number (or 這/那/幾) and the noun there must be a measure word.** At A1 there are no exceptions you need to know.

head: Measure word
Sound
Used for
Example
rows: ⚠️ anything, if you forget — neutral tone
一**杯**茶 a cup of tea
兩**瓶**水 two bottles of water
一**碗**麵 a bowl of noodles
一**份**便當 one lunch box
flat things: tables, paper, tickets, cards
一**件**衣服 a piece of clothing
long, bendy things: roads, pants, fish, dogs
五**口**人 five people (in a family)

blocks.title: ⚠️ Four lifesaving rules
items: **If you forget the measure word, use 個.** A small slip is far better than using none at all — that sounds like a robot.
**Required after 這, 那, and 幾 too.** 這**本**書 this book, 幾**個**人 how many people.
**兩, not 二, before a measure word.** 兩個人 two people, not 二個人. 二 is only for counting and for digits inside larger numbers.
**When the noun is clear, the noun can go but the measure word stays.** 我要三**個**。 "I'd like three."

blocks.text: Numbers

⚠️ **萬 = ten thousand, and Mandarin counts in groups of ten thousand, not a thousand.** One million isn't "a thousand thousand" but **一百萬** (a hundred ten-thousands). This takes time to adjust to, and there's no shortcut but practice. House prices and salaries in Taiwan are always given in 萬.

blocks.text: ⚠️ **Mandarin date order is always big to small**: year – month – date – weekday – part of day – hour. *二〇二六年五月十二號星期二下午三點* — "3 p.m., Tuesday, May 12, 2026". The order is roughly the reverse of English, and it applies to addresses too: country, city, street, house number, and only then the person's name.

back.title: Taiwan vs. mainland China: what's different

blocks.text: It's one language, but if you learned from a Beijing textbook and then live in Taipei, a few dozen everyday words will make you sound foreign. This list covers the most common ones.

head: Meaning
Taiwan 台灣
Mainland 大陸
Note
rows: ⚠️ 機車 also means "annoying" in slang
⚠️ 普通話 is hardly used in Taiwan

blocks.text: Distinctly Taiwanese ways of speaking

items: **不好意思** is used for almost everything**:** excuse me, sorry, may I ask, calling the waiter, and saying no politely. If you learn only one phrase from this book, make it this one.
**Plenty of sentence-final particles:** 啦, 喔, 耶, 欸, 齁, 嘛. Most come from Hokkien, and without them your sentences sound like official announcements. 好啦！ "OK, fine!" 對啊 "yeah, right".
**有 + verb** to ask whether something actually happened: 你**有**吃嗎？ "Did you eat?" ⚠️ Mainland grammar books call this wrong, but it's normal and everywhere in Taiwan.

**Some words are pronounced differently:** 和 (and) is read **hàn** by many Taiwanese, not *hé*; 垃圾 (trash) is read **lèsè**, not *lājī*; 而且 is *érqiě* in both places, but 期 in 星期 is **qí** in Taiwan, *qī* on the mainland.
**兒化 barely exists.** In Taiwan people say 這裡 *zhèlǐ*, not 这儿 *zhèr*; 一點 *yìdiǎn*, not 一点儿 *yìdiǎnr*.

blocks.text: Core words from the twenty units, in English alphabetical order. The unit number is given so you can go back to where the word first appears.

You've just completed level A1. That means you can look after yourself in Taiwan: order food, use public transportation, ask for directions, go shopping, visit a clinic, and get to know people. That's no small thing — most people who start learning Mandarin stop long before this point.
Four things that matter most over the next three months

items: **Fifteen minutes every day beats three hours every Sunday.** A tonal language needs an ear that's tended daily. Slip this book into the gaps of your day; don't schedule it like an exam.
**Listen to Taiwanese Mandarin, not mainland Mandarin.** The sounds differ and the vocabulary differs. Look for Taiwanese podcasts and dramas; your ear will tune itself to what it hears most.
**Handwrite ten characters a day.** Say the sounds out loud as you go. It's the cheapest way to stop characters feeling like random pictures.
**Start speaking sooner than feels right.** ⚠️ Waiting until you're "good enough" is the most common way never to start. Taiwanese people are famously kind to foreigners who try their language.

blocks.text: Where to go after A1

items: **A2** adds: longer stories about the past, comparisons, complaining and complimenting, office matters and renting a home, and about 700 characters.

**Taiwan's official exam is the 華語文能力測驗 (TOCFL)**, not the HSK. Levels A1–A2 correspond to TOCFL **Band A**. ⚠️ If you're aiming for a scholarship or study in Taiwan, it's the TOCFL they ask for, not the HSK.
**The Huayu Enrichment Scholarship (HES)** from Taiwan's Ministry of Education funds 2–12 months of language study in Taiwan, and A1 is already enough to apply.
**Linguo private classes** take this course on to A2 and beyond, with a teacher who can correct your tones on the spot — something no book can do.

blocks.title: One last sentence to take home
items: **萬事起頭難。** *Wàn shì qǐ tóu nán.* — "In all things, the beginning is the hardest part."
You've made it through the beginning. 加油！ *Jiāyóu!* — Keep going!
